title: Jonah and the Garden Anew
premise: Oscar Yarrow has spent years keeping her heart as carefully maintained as her late grandfather's lighthouse: functional, isolated, and never left on for anyone else. When the small coastal town's winter festival pairs anonymous pen-pals to raise money for the failing community garden, she's matched with a stranger whose letters slowly dismantle every wall she owns—until she discovers he is Elias Thorne, the developer whose resort project threatens both the garden and her family's lighthouse. Their letters become a battlefield of honesty and deception, each falling for the person behind the enemy while hiding their real identities. At the festival's closing night, when masks drop and the garden's fate is decided in a single vote, Oscar must choose between the publishing career that rescued her from grief and the man who finally sees her—choosing neither safely, but a third path they build together.
about_author: Ivo Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing lighthouse logs before turning to fiction full-time. They write love stories set against working coastlines, insisting that the best romances are built like seawalls: patiently, and to withstand weather.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. She maintains the decommissioned lighthouse, teaches herself emotional containment like a discipline, and hides her successful romance novels behind a pseudonym even from her found-family of townsfolk. The festival committee drafts her into the anonymous pen-pal fundraiser for the community garden. Beat: control established, cracks invisible.

chapters.title: Letters to No One
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, intercut with her correspondent's letters. Her first assigned letter goes out; the reply that returns is sharp, funny, and uncomfortably perceptive about her evasions. Meanwhile Elias Thorne arrives in town with resort blueprints and a smile nobody trusts. Beat: intrigue kindled; the reader sees what Oscar cannot.

chapters.title: Salt and Scaffolding
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He answers the pen-pal letters half as PR strategy, then finds himself telling a stranger truths he tells no one—including why he builds things and what it cost him. In town, he clashes publicly with Oscar over the garden survey. Beat: the enemy humanized; dramatic irony tightens.

chapters.title: What the Tide Brings
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A storm strands Elias at the lighthouse overnight; forced proximity produces a truce and an almost-confession neither completes. Afterward, his letters grow more intimate, and she realizes she's writing to someone who knows her without knowing her name. Beat: desire acknowledged, identity still hidden.

chapters.title: The Garden Vote
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The town council schedules the deciding vote on the resort for festival night. Elias's corporate backers pressure him; Oscar's found family rallies the garden volunteers. Both correspondents promise each other honesty 'before the festival ends.' Beat: stakes crystallize; clocks start ticking.

chapters.title: Manuscript and Mortar
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Her editor demands a new book by spring—the career that paid off her grandfather's debts—and offers a profile feature that would unmask her pseudonym. Torn, she nearly confesses everything in a letter, then loses her nerve. Beat: the price of survival made explicit; self-betrayal looms.

chapters.title: Every Wall Has a Door
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. His company leaks the resort plans early, framing the garden as expendable; he discovers his own signature authorized the press release he never read. Disgusted, he writes his pen-pal the whole truth except one name. Beat: power corrupts its own; his crisis of conscience peaks.

chapters.title: The Unmasking
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Festival eve: Oscar finds Elias's letter draft in the garden shed—his handwriting matching months of correspondence. Confrontation in the storm-dark greenhouse: fury, betrayal, and the terrible admission that she knew and stayed anyway. Beat: climax of revelation; both hearts exposed.

chapters.title: Voting Light
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Festival night. Elias publicly withdraws the resort and proposes a heritage trust preserving the lighthouse and garden instead, staking his career on it. Oscar takes the stage, claims her real name and her novels, and reads aloud their letters as evidence that people change. Beat: public choice over private safety.

chapters.title: Jonah and the Garden Anew
chapters.summary: Epilogue, dual POV. Spring: the garden blooms, the lighthouse relit as a writers' retreat where Oscar teaches, and Elias, unemployed by choice, learns to build slowly. A final exchanged letter, signed with real names this time. Beat: found family widened, survival redefined as choosing each other.
